title: The Mountain That Ate Men: Potosí and the Silver of the World
subtitle: The Cerro Rico of Potosí, Upper Peru (now Bolivia), from the strike of 1545 to the silver tide of 1600
intro: In April 1545 Spanish miners at Porco, in the high Andes of what was then called Upper Peru, registered claims on a red cone of a mountain some 4,000 metres up, in a cold, treeless puna where nothing grew but a little grass. Within a few years the camp at its foot, Potosí, was one of the largest towns in the Americas, and the Cerro Rico, the Rich Hill, was the single greatest source of silver in the world. Its silver paid for Spanish armies in Europe, passed through Seville into the money of Genoa, Antwerp and beyond, and crossed the Pacific on the Manila galleons after 1571 to be traded for Chinese silks and porcelain.

The finder of the mountain is usually named as an Andean man, Diego Huallpa (Acosta in 1590 calls him Gualpa, of the Chumbivilcas people near Cuzco), who is said to have caught hold of a bush while chasing deer and seen rich ore in its roots. The story reaches the page only through Spanish chroniclers writing decades later, and it was embroidered further in the eighteenth century. No surviving firsthand account by Huallpa, or by any of the Andean men who first worked the veins, has been found.

The honest record of Potosí in the sixteenth century is not a set of diaries. It is letters to the Council of the Indies and to Philip II, chronicles, a mine owner's report, a friar's memorial, the petitions of Andean lords, treasury registers summarised by chroniclers, and, later, the drawings of an Andean author. They are set here with their forms named plainly. Some of the most vivid voices, such as Guaman Poma de Ayala (c. 1615) and Bartolomé Arzáns de Orsúa y Vela (1700s), wrote after 1600 and are labelled as later or secondhand for these years.

Two technical and political changes turned a boom of the 1540s and 1550s into a system that lasted two and a half centuries. In the early 1570s the mercury amalgamation process, already used in New Spain, was brought to Potosí, using mercury from Huancavelica in central Peru; it made the lower-grade ores of the mountain profitable again. And Viceroy Francisco de Toledo organised the mita: a compulsory annual draft of Andean men aged about 18 to 50 from sixteen highland provinces, who were sent to Potosí to work in the mines and mills for low fixed wages. Figures for the size of the draft are given in this chapter as positions: about 13,500 a year in many accounts, 14,181 in the general allotment of 1578 as cited by one modern study, and 'over 11,000' in another reference work, with roughly a third working at any one time.

How many people died because of the mines is not known. Contemporaries described men crushed in falls, broken by carrying ore up hide ladders in the dark, and sickened by cold and by mercury; one friar wrote in 1586 that half of twenty healthy men going in on Monday might come out crippled by Sunday. Others fled their home villages to escape the draft. Later writers and modern historians give very different totals and causes (accidents, disease, epidemics, flight, mercury poisoning), and none of the large round numbers in circulation rests on a count. They are treated here as positions, not facts.

Set side by side, these eyes show the same mountain as a market and a mouth of hell, as a royal revenue and a sentence served by whole communities, as a marvel of devotion and as a reason why prices rose in Seville and Manila. The men who carried the ore left the fewest words; where their lords petitioned the king, their claims are given in their own documents.
calendar_note: Dates before October 1582 are Julian, as historians cite them. Spain adopted the Gregorian calendar in October 1582 and the Spanish Indies applied it over the following year or two; dates after that are Gregorian. Most sources in this chapter give only a year or a month, and entries say so in their precision field. Some entries are placed at the date of the event a chronicler describes rather than the date of writing; the digest then says when the account was written.

eyes.name: Pedro de Cieza de León
eyes.role: Spanish soldier and chronicler, about 31 when he visited Charcas and Potosí in 1549
eyes.where: Travelled through Peru; visited Porco and Potosí in 1549; published in Seville in 1553
eyes.vantage_label: eyewitness visitor of the boom years
eyes.authenticity: Parte primera de la Chronica del Peru was printed in Seville in 1553, the only part published in his lifetime. Clements Markham's English translation, The Travels of Pedro de Cieza de León (Hakluyt Society, 1864), is public domain; chapters CVIII–CX treat Porco and Potosí.
eyes.bio: Cieza went to the Indies as a boy and spent years as a soldier before turning to systematic note-taking on the lands and peoples of Peru. He saw Potosí only four years after the strike, when Andean smelters with small wind furnaces still did most of the refining. His account is the earliest substantial printed description of the town.

sources.title: The Travels of Pedro de Cieza de León (Markham, 1864), Project Gutenberg
Parte primera dela Chronica del Peru (Seville, 1553), Library of Congress, Kislak Collection

eyes.name: Fray Domingo de Santo Tomás
eyes.role: Dominican friar in Peru, linguist of Quechua, later bishop of Charcas (from 1563)
eyes.side: Spain; Dominican defenders of Andean rights
eyes.where: Peru; wrote to the Council of the Indies about Potosí in 1550 (place of writing not given in the excerpt consulted)
eyes.vantage_label: friar protesting to the Council of the Indies
eyes.authenticity: His letter of 1 July 1550 survives in the Archivo General de Indias (Lima 113) and was printed by José María Vargas (Quito, 1937). A draft English translation by Kris Lane (2018) is posted by the Friends of Potosí project at Tulane. The phrase 'mouth of hell' (boca del infierno) is his.
eyes.bio: Santo Tomás was one of the first Europeans to master Quechua; his grammar and dictionary were printed in Valladolid in 1560. His 1550 letter is the earliest sustained protest against forced labour at Potosí, written while the mountain was barely five years old.

sources.title: Friends of Potosí: The mines of Potosí, 1 July 1550 (translation index)
Domingo de Santo Tomás on Potosí (draft translation, PDF)

eyes.name: Juan de Matienzo
eyes.role: Judge (oidor) of the Audiencia of Charcas at La Plata
eyes.where: La Plata (now Sucre), about 150 km from Potosí
eyes.vantage_label: royal judge who drafted the case for compulsion
eyes.authenticity: Gobierno del Perú, completed in 1567, circulated in manuscript and was first printed in the twentieth century (modern edition by Guillermo Lohmann Villena, 1967). Date of completion is as given by its editors.
eyes.bio: Matienzo was one of the chief theorists of colonial rule in the Andes. His Gobierno del Perú argued that the mines could not be worked without a regular, compulsory rotation of Andean labourers and laid out rules for it, ideas Viceroy Toledo would put into practice.

sources.title: Gobierno del Perú (1567), ed. G. Lohmann Villena (Paris–Lima, 1967)

eyes.name: Francisco de Toledo
eyes.where: Lima; general inspection of the highlands, at Potosí in 1572–73 and La Plata in 1573–74
eyes.vantage_label: the viceroy who built the system
eyes.form: official records (ordinances and letters to the king)
eyes.authenticity: Toledo's letters to Philip II are in the Archivo General de Indias and were printed in Roberto Levillier's series Gobernantes del Perú (Madrid, 1921–26); his ordinances were compiled in Disposiciones gubernativas para el virreinato del Perú (modern ed., 1986–89). Exact days of individual letters and ordinances given here are approximate.
eyes.bio: Toledo, a Castilian nobleman and soldier, arrived in Peru in late 1569 with orders to restore royal revenue and control. He resettled Andean communities into reduction towns, took the Huancavelica mercury mine for the crown, backed amalgamation at Potosí and organised the Potosí mita. Andean writers, above all Guaman Poma, remembered him as the author of their ruin.

sources.title: Gobernantes del Perú: cartas y papeles del siglo XVI (Levillier), series page
Library of Congress blog: A short story about Potosí, part 2

eyes.name: José de Acosta
eyes.role: Jesuit priest and naturalist, in Peru 1572–1586; Jesuit provincial of Peru from 1576
eyes.where: Peru and Upper Peru 1572–86 (including Potosí); wrote in Mexico and Spain; published in Seville 1590
eyes.vantage_label: learned visitor reckoning the mountain's yield
eyes.authenticity: Historia natural y moral de las Indias, Seville, 1590; English by 'E.G.' (Edward Grimston), London, 1604, public domain. Book IV, chapters 6–12, cover the Cerro of Potosí, its discovery, yields, mining, refining and the mercury of Huancavelica. The registration dates and treasury totals he gives are his own, from records he says he consulted.
eyes.bio: Acosta was one of the most widely read writers on the Americas in early modern Europe. He gives the discovery story with names and dates, the totals of silver registered for the royal fifth, a precise description of the adits and ladders, and the history of amalgamation, all from a man who had been in Upper Peru under Toledo.

sources.title: Historia natural y moral de las Indias (Spanish text, PDF)
The Naturall and Morall Historie of the East and West Indies (London, 1604), Biodiversity Heritage Library

eyes.name: Luis Capoche
eyes.role: Spanish mine and refining-mill owner at Potosí
eyes.authenticity: Relación general de la villa imperial de Potosí, dated 1585, survived in manuscript and was first published by Lewis Hanke (Biblioteca de Autores Españoles, vol. 122, Madrid, 1959). Digests only; no published pre-1929 English translation.
eyes.bio: Capoche wrote as an insider: a refiner who knew the veins, the mills along the artificial lakes and the labour gangs. His report describes the mountain and its mills in detail and records the treatment of mita labourers, sometimes with sympathy, from the point of view of a man whose income depended on them.

sources.title: Relación general de la villa imperial de Potosí (1585), ed. Lewis Hanke, BAE 122 (1959)

eyes.name: The mallku (lords) of Charcas, signatories of the Memorial de Charcas
eyes.role: Hereditary Aymara and Quechua lords (caciques, kurakas) of the Qaraqara, Charka and allied nations of Upper Peru
eyes.side: Andean lordships subject to the mita
eyes.where: The provinces of Charcas, north and west of Potosí
eyes.authenticity: The Memorial de Charcas is usually dated to about 1582; it was published by Waldemar Espinoza Soriano (1969) and re-edited in T. Platt, T. Bouysse-Cassagne and O. Harris, Qaraqara-Charka (La Paz, 2006). The precise date and the full list of signatories should be checked against that edition.
eyes.bio: These lords had served the Inca and then the Spanish crown, and they led the men of their communities to Potosí under the mita. In their memorial they recounted their services, asked to be treated as nobles, and sought remedies for the burdens of the Toledan reforms. It is among the few sixteenth-century documents in which the communities that supplied mita labour speak through their own leaders.

sources.title: Review of Qaraqara-Charka (Chungara 41:2, 2009)

eyes.name: Fray Rodrigo de Loaysa
eyes.side: Spain; clerical critics of the mita
eyes.authenticity: His Memorial de las cosas del Perú tocantes a los indios (1586) is in Spanish archives and was printed in the Colección de documentos inéditos para la historia de España (vol. 94, 1889). Cited here through modern scholarship.
eyes.bio: Loaysa wrote a memorial on the abuses suffered by Andean people. His short description of what a week in the mines did to healthy men became one of the most quoted contemporary judgements on the Potosí mita.

sources.title: R. Gil Montero, 'Free and Unfree Labour in the Colonial Andes', International Review of Social History 56 (2011)

eyes.name: Fray Diego de Ocaña
eyes.role: Hieronymite monk of Guadalupe (Extremadura), collecting alms for his monastery and spreading the cult of the Virgin of Guadalupe
eyes.where: Travelled from Spain through Panama and Peru to Charcas; in Potosí 1600–01
eyes.vantage_label: travelling monk who painted and preached at Potosí
eyes.authenticity: His travel account (1599–1605), with his own drawings, survives in manuscript; it was first edited by Fray Arturo Álvarez and again by Beatriz Carolina Peña as Viaje por el Nuevo Mundo: de Guadalupe a Potosí, 1599–1605. Months for his Potosí entries come from secondary summaries and are approximate.
eyes.bio: Ocaña arrived at the height of Potosí's wealth, painted an image of the Virgin of Guadalupe for the town, and wrote of the mountain with wonder. His account gives the rare view of a newcomer at the turn of the century, when the Toledan system was a generation old.

sources.title: Correo del Sur: Guadalupe en Potosí (2018)
Viaje por el Nuevo Mundo: de Guadalupe a Potosí, 1599–1605 (catalogue record)

eyes.name: Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala
eyes.role: Andean noble of Lucanas (Ayacucho region), interpreter and author
eyes.where: Lucanas and Huamanga; travelled to Lima c. 1615
eyes.authenticity: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno, c. 1615, a 1,189-page autograph manuscript addressed to Philip III, is in the Royal Danish Library, Copenhagen (GKS 2232 4º), fully digitised. Written decades after Toledo; it is labelled here as a later Andean account of the sixteenth century.
eyes.bio: Guaman Poma wrote and drew a vast letter to the king denouncing colonial abuses, with nearly 400 drawings. His pages on Huancavelica and Potosí show the mines as places of suffering and the silver as the support of Castile; he names Toledo as a destroyer of Andean order. He is the closest the record comes to an Andean eye on the mita, though not that of a mine worker himself.

sources.title: Royal Danish Library: Guaman Poma, Nueva corónica y buen gobierno (digital edition)
Drawing 370: the mercury mines of Huancavelica (page 1055)

eyes.name: Bartolomé Arzáns de Orsúa y Vela
eyes.role: Creole chronicler born and living in Potosí
eyes.vantage_label: later chronicler of his own town (secondhand for the 1500s)
eyes.authenticity: Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, a manuscript continued until his death in 1736 (and by his son), was published in full by Lewis Hanke and Gunnar Mendoza (Providence, 1965). For the sixteenth century it is secondhand, mixing records, oral tradition, legend and invention; its figures are not reliable as counts.
eyes.bio: Arzáns wrote the town's great baroque history, full of duels, miracles, fortunes and ruin. His account of the discovery and of the early decades shaped the popular image of Potosí, including the Huallpa legend, and is valuable chiefly as Potosí's memory of itself.

sources.title: Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, ed. L. Hanke and G. Mendoza (1965)

eyes.name: Tomás de Mercado
eyes.role: Dominican theologian who had lived in Mexico, writing on commerce for the merchants of Seville
eyes.where: Seville, the port where American silver landed
eyes.authenticity: Tratos y contratos de mercaderes (Salamanca, 1569), expanded as Suma de tratos y contratos (Seville, 1571). Printed editions survive; modern editions and digitised texts exist.
eyes.bio: Mercado wrote a practical moral guide for traders on the steps of Seville cathedral. He observed that money from the Indies was worth less in Spain than in Flanders or Rome, and his discussion of exchange and prices is read today as an early account of what American silver did to European money.

sources.title: Suma de tratos y contratos (Spanish text, PDF)
A. Giráldez, 'La primera globalización y un inquisidor en el Potosí de 1650', eHumanista 7 (2006)

eyes.name: Domingo de Salazar
eyes.side: Spain; the Church in the Philippines
eyes.vantage_label: at the Pacific end of the silver road
eyes.authenticity: His letters to Philip II survive in the Archivo General de Indias and were translated in E. H. Blair and J. A. Robertson, The Philippine Islands, 1493–1898 (55 vols., 1903–09), vol. 7, now on Project Gutenberg; short quotations here are from that translation.
eyes.bio: Salazar ministered to the Chinese merchants and craftsmen of Manila's Parián and wrote at length to the king about them. His letters show the Chinese side of the silver trade from the Spanish bishop's desk: who sold, who bought, and what money from Mexico did to prices.

sources.title: Blair and Robertson, The Philippine Islands, vol. 7 (1588–1591), Project Gutenberg
Plain text of vol. 7

eyes.name: Gaspar de Ayala
eyes.role: Royal attorney (fiscal) of the Audiencia of Manila
eyes.vantage_label: crown official watching Peruvian money reach China
eyes.authenticity: His letter to Philip II of 15 July 1589 is translated in Blair and Robertson, vol. 7. His office is as described in that collection.
eyes.bio: Ayala wrote as a royal lawyer worried that direct trade from Peru and New Spain to China would drain the colony. His letter records a Peruvian or Panamanian ship arriving at Macao with a large sum of money, a glimpse of Potosí silver going straight to Chinese markets.

sources.title: Blair and Robertson, The Philippine Islands, vol. 7 (1588–1591), Project Gutenberg

entries.date_display: 21 April 1545 (Julian), as given by Acosta in 1590
entries.place: Porco and the Cerro of Potosí (written in 1590)
entries.headline: An Andean hunter's handful of ore becomes the first registered claim
entries.digest: Writing forty-five years later, Acosta tells how an Indian he calls Gualpa, of the Chumbivilcas people near Cuzco, caught a branch while chasing deer up the hill and saw rich metal in its roots. Gualpa had the ore assayed at Porco and worked it secretly until a neighbour, Guanca from the Jauja valley, pressed him and was given a vein of his own. After a quarrel Guanca told his Spanish master, Villarroel, who went to the hill and staked claims; Acosta dates the first registration at Porco to 21 April 1545.
entries.source_note: Acosta, Historia natural y moral de las Indias (1590), Book IV ch. 6. The date is Acosta's; the story is a tradition reported decades after the event.

entries.headline: The town's chronicler turns the discovery into legend
entries.digest: Arzáns, writing in Potosí more than 150 years later, retells the finding of the mountain by the Indian Diego Huallpa and surrounds it with legend, including an Inca-era tale of a voice from the hill forbidding the Incas to dig because the silver was meant for others. His version became the popular one. It is a later chronicle built on tradition and cannot stand as a record of 1545.
entries.source_note: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, ed. Hanke and Mendoza (1965), opening books. Details of his version summarised from general knowledge of the edition; not checked page by page.

entries.headline: The fourth great vein, the Mendieta, is registered
entries.digest: Acosta lists the four principal veins of the hill: the Rica, found first; the Centeno, which Gualpa gave to Guanca; the Estaño; and the Mendieta, registered on 31 August 1545. Within months, he implies, the rush had begun, with Spaniards and great numbers of Indians from many provinces flocking to the cold slope.
entries.source_note: Acosta, Historia natural y moral (1590), Book IV ch. 6.

entries.headline: Thousands of little wind furnaces glitter on the hills at night
entries.digest: Cieza found that Spanish bellows furnaces failed in the thin air of Potosí, and that the silver was being smelted by Andean workers in small clay furnaces called huayras, pierced with holes and set on the windy ridges. At night the hillsides were dotted with their fires. He presents the technique as an Inca invention without which the mountain could not have been worked.
entries.quote: the Indians get it by the invention of the huayras
entries.source_note: Cieza, Crónica del Perú part 1 (1553), ch. CIX; Markham trans. (1864), chapter title. Year of his visit from Markham's introduction.

entries.headline: A boom-town market where everything comes on human backs
entries.digest: Cieza describes the market at the foot of the hill, where Andean traders, many of them women, sold food, coca, clothing and goods brought from great distances, and where the turnover astonished him. In a place where nothing grew, the whole town lived on what was carried in. He calls it the richest market in the world while the mines were prospering.
entries.quote: the richest market in the world at this hill of Potosi
entries.source_note: Cieza, Crónica del Perú part 1 (1553), ch. CX; Markham trans. (1864), chapter title. Detail of goods paraphrased from the chapter's subject; figures for turnover not checked.

entries.place: Peru, letter to the Council of the Indies
entries.headline: A friar names Potosí a mouth of hell
entries.digest: Santo Tomás tells the Council that about four years earlier a mouth of hell had opened in the land, which swallows a great many people every year, sacrificed by Spanish greed to their god. He insists that reports of Indians thriving in the mines are true only of some yanaconas, the dependent servants of Spaniards, and not of the men sent there under compulsion.
entries.source_note: Letter of 1 July 1550, AGI Lima 113; ed. J. M. Vargas (1937), pp. 15–21; draft English trans. K. Lane (2018), Friends of Potosí.

entries.headline: Men marched 180 leagues to a hill with no firewood
entries.digest: In the same letter he describes a hill in a cold, barren country with no plants for six leagues around, where charcoal, food and fuel had to be carried in on human backs or by llama. Wheat, maize, chuño and potatoes sold at very high prices. Under the repartimiento, Indians were sent from as far as 180 leagues in parties of 50, 100, 200 and more; he argues that driving free people this way is fit only for slaves or condemned criminals, against the king's own ordinances.
entries.source_note: Letter of 1 July 1550, as above.

entries.date_display: c. 1549–1551, 'in the time of licenciado Polo', as reported by Acosta
entries.place: Potosí, royal smelting and assay house (written in 1590)
entries.headline: Saturday registrations of up to 200,000 pesos
entries.digest: Acosta reports that in the early years, under the licenciado Polo, the silver brought every Saturday for registration and taxing came to 150,000 or 200,000 pesos, of which the royal fifth was 30,000 to 40,000. That made about a million and a half a year. He adds that much silver escaped registration altogether.
entries.source_note: Acosta, Historia natural y moral (1590), Book IV ch. 7. The years of Polo's tenure are not pinned down here.

entries.headline: Europe first reads of Potosí in print
entries.digest: Cieza's Parte primera de la Chronica del Peru was printed in Seville, with woodcuts made by artists who had never seen the Andes, among them a view of the Cerro of Potosí. For many European readers this was the first account of the silver hill. Cieza died the following year in Seville, leaving later parts of his chronicle unpublished.
entries.source_note: Library of Congress Kislak copy (1553 edition); LOC blog on Potosí (2022); Brown University JCB note on the 1553 woodcuts.

entries.headline: Work begins on a tunnel that will take 29 years
entries.digest: Acosta records that the Venino adit, a horizontal tunnel about eight feet wide driven into the hill to meet the veins, was begun in 1556. Owners of such adits took a fifth of any ore drawn out through them. The project shows how quickly the easy surface ores gave way to deep, slow, dangerous work.
entries.source_note: Acosta, Historia natural y moral (1590), Book IV ch. 8.

entries.headline: The friar's Quechua grammar is printed in Spain
entries.digest: Santo Tomás's grammar and dictionary of Quechua, the general language of Peru, were printed in Valladolid. The books were meant for priests, but they also recorded the language of the men drafted to Potosí. He returned to Upper Peru as bishop of Charcas a few years later.
entries.source_note: Grammatica o arte de la lengua general de los indios de los reynos del Peru and Lexicon (Valladolid, 1560); standard bibliographies.

entries.headline: A judge argues the mines need forced rotation
entries.digest: By the 1560s the rich surface ores were exhausted, output was falling and voluntary labour was scarce. Matienzo's Gobierno del Perú argues that the crown should require Andean communities to send a regular share of their men to the mines in rotation, under rules on pay and duration. He presents compulsion as necessary for the kingdom and beneficial to the Indians, a claim the Andean lords and many friars rejected.
entries.source_note: Matienzo, Gobierno del Perú (1567), ed. Lohmann Villena (1967), part I chapters on mines. Chapter detail not checked against the edition.

entries.headline: A friar writes a moral guide for silver merchants
entries.digest: Mercado published Tratos y contratos de mercaderes, a guide for the traders of Seville on just prices, exchanges and loans. He wrote for a city whose wealth rose and fell with the arrival of the fleets from the Indies, and whose merchants had to decide what was honest when money itself kept changing value.
entries.source_note: First edition Salamanca, 1569; standard bibliographies.

entries.headline: Silver is worth more in Flanders and Rome than in Spain
entries.digest: In the expanded Suma de tratos y contratos printed in Seville, Mercado compared money markets across Europe and found that silver bought more in Flanders and Rome than in Spain. He explained the favourable exchange abroad by the higher value of money there. Modern economists read the observation as an early recognition that the flood of American silver was lowering its value at home.
entries.source_note: Mercado, Suma de tratos y contratos (Seville, 1571); as summarised in Giráldez, eHumanista 7 (2006), citing Sayous.

entries.headline: Mercury comes to Potosí and the mountain revives
entries.digest: Acosta records that the refining of silver with mercury began at Potosí in 1571, under Viceroy Toledo, brought by Pero Fernández de Velasco, who had seen it used in New Spain. Ore was ground fine, mixed with mercury and salt, and the mercury then driven off by heat, recovering silver from ores that smelting could not pay for. Acosta treats the change as the rebirth of Potosí; other sources place Velasco's demonstration in 1572.
entries.source_note: Acosta, Historia natural y moral (1590), Book IV ch. 12; LOC blog (2022) gives 1572.

entries.headline: The viceroy takes the mercury mountain for the crown
entries.digest: Toledo expropriated the Huancavelica mercury district for the crown and contracted mine operators to produce mercury at a fixed price, promising them a draft of cheap forced labour. Huancavelica would supply nearly all the mercury used by Peruvian silver refiners for two centuries. Its miners breathed mercury dust and vapour, and as workers died or fled, the provinces that served it emptied.
entries.source_note: Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture, 'Huancavelica' (encyclopedia.com). Toledo's own decrees not consulted directly.

entries.headline: The viceroy arrives at the mountain
entries.digest: On his long inspection of the highlands, Toledo reached Potosí late in 1572 and stayed into 1573. He met the mine owners, saw the amalgamation trials and studied how to supply labour, water and mercury. He divided the towns of the mita region into districts each to send about one-seventh of its able-bodied men every year, under captains of the mita.
entries.source_note: LOC blog (2022): 1572 division into districts sending about 1/7 of able men, five capitanes de mita. Arrival month approximate, from standard histories (Bakewell).

entries.headline: Toledo reports to the king without waiting for leave
entries.digest: From Potosí Toledo wrote to Philip II on the state of the mines, amalgamation and labour. He organised the forced draft without prior royal approval, presenting it as a revival of an Inca labour service and as the only way to save the king's revenue. The king's councils debated the morality of compulsion for years afterward while the draft ran.
entries.source_note: Toledo's letters in Levillier, Gobernantes del Perú; Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture, 'Mita' (crown approval not sought). The specific letter and day are not confirmed here.

entries.place: Potosí and the sixteen mita provinces
entries.headline: The first contingents of the Potosí mita march
entries.digest: Men aged roughly 18 to 50 from the highland provinces between Cuzco and Potosí were drafted for a year's service, often walking for weeks with their families and llamas. At Potosí they were divided into three groups, each working a week and resting two, in mines and mills, for wages a fraction of what free workers earned. Many accounts give the annual draft as about 13,500 men.
entries.source_note: DIA, University of Pennsylvania, 'Mita' (about 13,500; 16 captaincies; thirds; ages 18–50). Annual figure contested; see claims ledger.

entries.headline: Mining ordinances set the rules of the system
entries.digest: From La Plata Toledo issued ordinances for the mines of Potosí, regulating claims, adits, refining mills, the lakes and dams that powered them, and the treatment, wages and duties of mita labourers. The rules gave the mine and mill owners a guaranteed workforce and bound them to obligations that were often ignored.
entries.source_note: Toledo, Ordenanzas de minas (La Plata, 1574), in Disposiciones gubernativas para el virreinato del Perú. Month from standard histories; not verified here.

entries.headline: Seventy-six million pesos in the books so far
entries.digest: Acosta reports that when Toledo had the royal accounts reviewed, the silver registered at Potosí from the discovery to 1574 came to 76 million pesos. He presents the figure as a minimum, since unregistered silver was never counted. The number became a European byword for the riches of Peru.
entries.source_note: Acosta, Historia natural y moral (1590), Book IV ch. 7.

entries.headline: The general allotment fixes the draft at 14,181
entries.digest: Toledo's general allotment of mita labour set the number of men owed to Potosí each year by each province. One modern study gives the total as 14,181, with more than 14,000 men and their families to come at below-market wages. Later allotments fell steeply as the drafted provinces lost people.
entries.source_note: Gil Montero, IRSH 56 (2011), citing the 1578 repartimiento general; later totals 12,354 (1633), 5,658 (1688), 4,101 (1692).

entries.headline: The lords of Charcas set out their services and grievances
entries.digest: The hereditary lords of the Qaraqara, Charka and allied nations addressed the king. They recounted how they and their ancestors had served the Inca and then the Spanish crown, in war and in labour, and asked to be treated with the honours of Spanish nobles. They sought remedies for the conditions the Toledan reforms had brought on their people, conditions that included the annual march of their men to Potosí.
entries.source_note: Memorial de Charcas, ed. Espinoza Soriano (1969) and Platt, Bouysse-Cassagne and Harris, Qaraqara-Charka (2006); content summarised from the 2009 Chungara review. Date conventional.

entries.headline: A refiner maps the mountain, its veins and its mills
entries.digest: Capoche describes Potosí as a cold, sterile, almost uninhabitable place where little grew but some potatoes, and yet the largest town in the kingdom. He lists the mines and the water-driven refining mills along the channel fed by the artificial lakes built above the town, and explains the amalgamation process step by step. His report was written for the crown by a man defending the owners' interests.
entries.source_note: Capoche, Relación general (1585), ed. Hanke (1959); description of the setting as quoted in Gil Montero (2011). Further contents summarised from the edition's known scope.

entries.headline: A mine owner records how the mitayos are worn down
entries.digest: Capoche records the labour of the drafted men: carrying sacks of ore up long ladders of hide in the dark, working by candlelight, and being paid below the wages of free workers. He acknowledges abuses, including forced extra shifts and the burdens that fell on the men's families. His concern is partly humane and partly practical: a workforce destroyed could not be replaced.
entries.source_note: Capoche, Relación general (1585), ed. Hanke (1959); labour conditions corroborated in Gil Montero (2011): 45 kg sacks, quota of 25 a day.

entries.headline: The Venino tunnel reaches the Rica vein after 29 years
entries.digest: Acosta records that the Venino adit, begun in 1556, was finished on 11 April 1585, meeting the Rica vein 35 estados below the surface. He describes the deep workings beside it: shafts 180 to 200 estados deep, porters climbing hide-rope ladders three at a time with loads of about two arrobas, the leader carrying a candle tied to his thumb.
entries.source_note: Acosta, Historia natural y moral (1590), Book IV ch. 8.

entries.headline: One hundred and eleven million pesos registered by 1585
entries.digest: Acosta adds 35 million pesos registered from 1574 to 1585 to the earlier 76 million, for 111 million pesos of assayed silver taxed since the discovery. The king, he says, was then receiving about a million pesos a year from the royal fifth alone. Unregistered silver, he notes again, is not in these sums.
entries.source_note: Acosta, Historia natural y moral (1590), Book IV ch. 7.

entries.headline: Twenty healthy men go in on Monday
entries.digest: Loaysa wrote that if twenty healthy Indians entered the mines on Monday, half might come out crippled by Sunday. His memorial describes the mita as a ruin of the drafted communities. It is a judgement of what he saw and heard, not a count of deaths, and it has been quoted ever since by critics of the system.
entries.source_note: Loaysa, Memorial de las cosas del Perú tocantes a los indios (1586), CODOIN vol. 94; as quoted in Gil Montero (2011).

entries.headline: The bishop wants direct Mexico–China trade stopped
entries.digest: Salazar complained to Philip II about the viceroy of New Spain's handling of the Manila trade, including the sale of a ship to a Mexican merchant for trade with China. He wanted the direct Mexico-to-China traffic stopped, so that trade, and the American silver that paid for it, passed through Manila.
entries.source_note: Salazar to Felipe II, Manila, 27 June 1588; Blair and Robertson vol. 7.

entries.headline: A ship from Peru with a fortune in money reaches Macao
entries.digest: Ayala reported that a ship from Panama or Peru, ready to lay out a large sum of money, had arrived at Portuguese Macao on the China coast. He warned that if trade between Peru or New Spain and China were allowed, the Philippines would be emptied of settlers. He also asked for forty or fifty thousand pesos to be sent yearly from New Spain to support the colony.
entries.quote: this country will be depopulated and ruined.
entries.source_note: Gaspar de Ayala to Felipe II, Manila, 15 July 1589; Blair and Robertson vol. 7 (English trans., 1903–09).

entries.headline: The Jesuit's natural history puts Potosí before Europe
entries.digest: Acosta's Historia natural y moral de las Indias appeared in Seville. His chapters on Potosí join the discovery tradition, the treasury totals, mining technique and the chemistry of mercury in one account, and they were translated into Italian, French, German, Dutch and English within a few years. Much of what Europe knew of the mountain came from these pages.
entries.source_note: Historia natural y moral de las Indias (Seville, 1590).

entries.headline: Chinese merchants, and prices that follow Mexican silver
entries.digest: Salazar described the Parián, the Chinese quarter of Manila, home to some three to four thousand Sangleys, with two thousand more coming and going on the ships. Its shops sold silks and linens, and its craftsmen worked as tailors, silversmiths, painters, bookbinders and bakers. A labourer earned a real a day; prices rose and fell with the money that arrived from Mexico, and the Sangleys raised them when buyers had silver.
entries.quote: The Sangleys are hard workers and very greedy for money.
entries.source_note: Salazar, 'The Chinese and the Parián at Manila', 24 June 1590; Blair and Robertson vol. 7 (English trans., 1903–09).

entries.headline: The eighth wonder of the world, worked by candlelight
entries.digest: Ocaña called the hill of Potosí the eighth wonder of the world and wrote that 8,000 Indians worked inside it every day by the light of tallow candles. He recorded a collapse in which five Indians were buried for five days and came out alive, which the faithful credited to the Virgin. Wonder and danger sit side by side in his pages.
entries.source_note: Ocaña, relación de viaje (1599–1605), as quoted in Correo del Sur (2 Sept 2018). Exact folio and date not checked.

entries.headline: A monk paints the Virgin for the silver town
entries.digest: Asked by the townspeople for a large image of the Virgin of Guadalupe, Ocaña painted one himself; it was set on the high altar of the Franciscan church with great festivities. The devotion spread through Charcas, and the image was still venerated in Potosí in 1616.
entries.source_note: Book of miracles cited by Arturo Álvarez, as summarised in Correo del Sur (2018); the article also gives 1601 for the first image, so the month is uncertain.

entries.headline: Forty-four bars of silver for a monastery in Spain
entries.digest: From the alms collected in Potosí and Charcas, Ocaña sent 44 bars of silver to his monastery of Guadalupe in Extremadura. It is a small, concrete instance of how Potosí silver reached Spain not only as royal fifths and merchants' bullion but as piety.
entries.source_note: Correo del Sur (2018), summarising Ocaña's papers.

entries.headline: Acosta's Potosí chapters appear in English
entries.digest: Edward Grimston's translation, The Naturall and Morall Historie of the East and West Indies, was printed in London. English readers, whose privateers had been raiding Spanish silver fleets, could now read the yields of Potosí and the mercury of Huancavelica in their own language. Acosta had died in 1600.
entries.source_note: The Naturall and Morall Historie (London: Val. Sims for E. Blount and W. Aspley, 1604), BHL record.

entries.headline: An Andean author draws the mercury mines of Huancavelica
entries.digest: In drawing 370 of his chronicle, Guaman Poma shows the mercury mines of Huancavelica and captions them as places where Indians suffer great hardships; a marginal note also names silver mines near Potosí. Writing decades after Toledo, he presents the mines as one of the main engines of Andean suffering under Spanish rule.
entries.source_note: Nueva corónica y buen gobierno, p. 1047 [1055], drawing 370; Royal Danish Library GKS 2232 4º.

entries.headline: Potosí drawn as the crowned support of Castile
entries.digest: Guaman Poma's drawing of the rich imperial town of Potosí places the town under the arms of the Spanish monarchy, with Latin and Quechua inscriptions, and his text presents the mountain as what sustained Castile. Elsewhere in the chronicle he condemns the mita and its abuses by Spanish officials, priests and Andean lords alike. It is a later Andean judgement on the sixteenth century, not a firsthand account of the 1570s.
entries.source_note: Nueva corónica, drawing 'La villa rica imperial de Potosí' (Linkgua visual archive; KB digital edition). Text paraphrased from the drawing's known caption and context; page not checked.

entries.headline: The man who 'ruined' the Andes, in Andean eyes
entries.digest: Guaman Poma writes of Viceroy Toledo as a destroyer of the Andean order: the reduction towns, the execution of the last Inca ruler Túpac Amaru in 1572 and the forced labour drafts. He urges the king to protect Andean communities and their lords. His view is the reverse of Toledo's own claim that he had restored order and saved the king's revenue.
entries.source_note: Nueva corónica y buen gobierno, sections on the viceroys (Toledo). Summarised from the work's well-known content; pages not checked.

entries.headline: Potosí's own chronicler weighs the cost of the silver
entries.digest: Over three decades Arzáns compiled his history of the Villa Imperial, year by year, from documents, earlier chronicles and stories still told in the town. He wrote of the mita and the deaths in the mountain with pity and moral alarm, but his large numbers for the early population and its losses mix record and rhetoric and are not reliable counts. His history is the town's memory of its sixteenth century, set down long after.
entries.source_note: Arzáns, Historia de la Villa Imperial de Potosí, ed. Hanke and Mendoza (1965), introduction. Not checked page by page.

claims.claim: First registration of a claim on the Cerro of Potosí, at Porco, by the Spaniard Villarroel with the Indian Guanca; the vein (la Rica) first found by the Indian Gualpa
claims.evidence: As reported by Acosta, Historia natural y moral (1590), IV.6; the original register not consulted

claims.claim: Mendieta vein registered, the last of the four principal veins (Rica, Centeno, Estaño, Mendieta)
Weekly Saturday registrations of 150,000–200,000 pesos, royal fifth 30,000–40,000; about 1.5 million pesos a year
claims.evidence: Acosta (1590), IV.7, from treasury records 'in the time of licenciado Polo'

claims.claim: Indians driven to Potosí from up to 180 leagues away in parties of 50 to 200 and more under the repartimiento

Discovery of the Huancavelica mercury deposit: Acosta credits the Portuguese Enrique Garcés c. 1566–67; other accounts credit Amador de Cabrera in 1563, led there by the kuraka Gonzalo Ñavincopa, whose people already knew the site
claims.evidence: Acosta (1590), IV.11; Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture, 'Huancavelica'

claims.claim: Mercury amalgamation introduced at Potosí by Pero Fernández de Velasco under Viceroy Toledo
Huancavelica mercury district expropriated for the crown; operators contracted at a fixed mercury price with mita labour
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture, 'Huancavelica'

claims.claim: Potosí mita organised: about one-seventh of the able men of sixteen provinces each year, about 13,500 men in many accounts (positions range from 'over 11,000' to 14,181), serving in three shifts
claims.evidence: DIA (UPenn), 'Mita'; LOC blog (2022); Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture, 'Mita'

claims.claim: 76 million pesos of silver registered at Potosí from the discovery to 1574, by Toledo's review of the accounts
General allotment of mita labour fixed at 14,181 men a year
Venino adit completed after 29 years (begun 1556), reaching the Rica vein at 35 estados
111 million pesos ensayados registered since 1545 (35 million more since 1574); royal fifth about 1 million pesos a year
Of twenty healthy Indians entering the mines on Monday, half may come out crippled by Sunday (a judgement, not a count)
claims.evidence: Loaysa, Memorial (1586), CODOIN 94; quoted in Gil Montero (2011)

claims.claim: A ship from Panama or Peru with a large sum of money arrived at Macao to trade directly with China
claims.evidence: Ayala to Felipe II, Blair and Robertson vol. 7

claims.claim: 8,000 Indians working inside the Cerro every day by tallow candlelight
claims.evidence: Ocaña, relación de viaje, quoted in Correo del Sur (2018)

claims.claim: 44 bars of silver sent from Potosí alms to the monastery of Guadalupe, Spain
claims.evidence: Correo del Sur (2018), from Ocaña's papers

convergences.label: The finding of the mountain
convergences.note: Both name an Andean finder and both write long after the event: Acosta in 1590 with registration dates from records, Arzáns in the 1700s with legend and prophecy. Neither preserves a word from Gualpa or Huallpa himself.

convergences.label: Market or mouth of hell: the boom years seen from inside
convergences.note: Within a year of each other Cieza marvels at the richest market in the world and the furnaces on the hills, while Santo Tomás sees a mouth of hell fed by forced drafts; Acosta later supplies the weekly treasury figures of the same years.

convergences.label: Mercury at Potosí, money in Seville
convergences.note: As amalgamation was tried at Potosí under Toledo, Mercado in Seville was noting that silver was worth less in Spain than abroad: the two ends of the same flow, one technical and one monetary.

convergences.label: The mita begins
convergences.note: Matienzo had argued for compulsory rotation; Toledo imposed it; the lords of Charcas, whose men marched, petitioned for remedies; Guaman Poma, a generation later, remembered Toledo as the destroyer of Andean order.

convergences.label: The mountain at full output
convergences.note: In the same two years a mine owner describes the mills and the labour, a Jesuit records 111 million pesos and the completion of a 29-year tunnel, and a friar writes that half of twenty healthy men might be crippled in a week.

convergences.label: Peruvian silver across the Pacific (1589–1590)
convergences.note: In Manila, Ayala warns of Peruvian money reaching Macao and Salazar sees prices follow Mexican silver in the Parián, while in Seville Acosta's book announces the mountain's riches to Europe.

convergences.label: A generation into the system
convergences.note: Fifteen years after Capoche's report, the newcomer Ocaña sees thousands working by candlelight and calls the hill a wonder; the owner and the monk describe the same labour from opposite moods.

ties.note: Matienzo's Gobierno del Perú (1567) proposed the compulsory labour rotation and rules that Toledo put into effect in 1572–78; Matienzo served in the Audiencia of Charcas under Toledo.
The viceroy fixed the quotas of men their communities owed to Potosí; the lords petitioned the king for remedies against the burdens of his reforms.
Toledo presented his reforms as restoring order; Guaman Poma, writing c. 1615, condemned him as the author of the Andean world's ruin.
Santo Tomás protested forced drafts to Potosí in 1550 and died in 1570; within three years Toledo made the forced draft the foundation of the mines.
Acosta was in Peru during Toledo's government and records his review of the treasury accounts and the introduction of amalgamation under him.
A mine owner and a friar described the same mine labour within a year of each other: one to defend the industry while admitting abuses, the other to condemn the system.
Both describe men carrying ore by candlelight in the same mountain, fifteen years apart.
The bishop and the royal attorney both wrote to Philip II from Manila in 1588–90 about the Chinese trade that American silver paid for.
Arzáns's discovery story builds on the tradition of the Andean finder that Acosta had set down in 1590, adding legend.
Both books were printed in Seville, the port of the silver fleets: Mercado's on what the money did to merchants, Acosta's on where it came from.
Both are Andean voices petitioning the Spanish king about the mita; Guaman Poma also criticises Andean lords who profited from the drafts.

threads_out.note: The amalgamation process brought to Potosí in the early 1570s had been developed in New Spain in the 1550s, in the mining country opened after the fall of Tenochtitlan; Pero Fernández de Velasco learned it there.

Mercury amalgamation, the technique that remade Potosí, was still the heart of silver and gold refining three centuries later; California's New Almaden quicksilver mine, named after Spain's Almadén, supplied the mercury of the Gold Rush and the Comstock.

American silver shipped through Manila from 1571 flowed into the Ming economy, which had come to rely on silver for taxes; the fall in silver inflows in the 1630s is one of the factors historians weigh in the Ming collapse.
Mercado's observation in 1571 that American silver had lost value in Spain is an early account of the price revolution, a forerunner of later thinking about money and inflation.

vantage_key: 0 = principal actors and the drafted communities (the viceroy, a mine owner, the Andean lords); 1 = visitors and clerics on the mountain; 2 = in Upper Peru or the town but at a remove in office or time; 3 = an Andean author elsewhere in Peru, writing later; 4 = at the far ends of the silver road, in Seville and Manila.
